questions.q: In a token bucket limiter, what does the bucket capacity control?
options: The steady-state request rate allowed over long time periods
How long a client must wait after a single rejected request
The number of distinct clients a single bucket can track
The maximum burst size allowed above the steady refill rate

questions.q: In a token bucket, what does the refill rate correspond to?
options: The sustained average request rate permitted over time
The maximum instantaneous burst the limiter will accept
The interval between full resets of every client's bucket
The penalty duration applied to clients exceeding quota

questions.q: Which status code signals a rate-limited HTTP request?
options: 403, indicating the client's credentials were revoked
503, indicating the entire service is currently unavailable
429, optionally paired with Retry-After guidance
409, indicating the request conflicts with another one

questions.q: What is the leaky bucket's defining behavior?
options: It permits unlimited instantaneous bursts as long as the daily total stays within quota
Requests drain at a constant rate, smoothing bursts into a steady flow
It multiplies each client's allowance whenever the system is idle
It rejects all traffic for a cooldown period after any single breach

questions.q: What is the classic flaw of a fixed window counter?
options: Bursts at a window boundary can allow nearly double the intended rate
It needs floating-point math, which drifts over long uptimes
It cannot be implemented in Redis without server-side scripting
Counters must be stored separately per URL path, which explodes memory usage quickly

questions.q: Why rate limit per API key or user rather than only globally?
options: Global limits are prohibited by most cloud providers' API terms
Per-key limits remove the need for authenticating requests entirely
One noisy client can otherwise consume the shared quota and starve others
Per-key limits make every response automatically cacheable at CDN edge locations

questions.q: What does the sliding window log approach store?
options: One counter per client, decayed exponentially every second
Timestamps of recent requests, pruned as they age out of the window
A fixed boolean flag per window marking whether the client exceeded its quota there
The average latency of each client's requests in the window

questions.q: Where is a rate limiter most commonly enforced?
options: Inside the database, by throttling slow queries per connection
In the client SDK, which the server trusts to self-report its usage
At the DNS layer, by delaying resolution for overly hot clients
At the API gateway or edge, before requests reach backend services

questions.q: Sliding window counter (two weighted windows) vs a full log: what do you give up?
options: It rejects far more legitimate traffic than any other algorithm
It requires synchronized clocks across every client device
Exactness: it approximates the rolling count using far less memory
It cannot express limits over any interval shorter than a full minute of wall time

questions.q: A distributed limiter keeps per-node local counters with no synchronization. What is the effect?
options: Each node rejects all traffic as soon as any node's counter fills
The limit still gets enforced globally as long as the load balancer is strictly round-robin
Requests queue at the load balancer until the counters synchronize
A client can reach roughly N times the limit by spreading requests across nodes

questions.q: You centralize counters in Redis. What are the main new risks?
options: Redis silently rounds all counters to powers of two, loosening every configured limit
Added latency per request and a dependency that can fail or hotspot
Counters can never expire, so memory grows without any bound
Atomic increments become impossible, so counts are always stale

questions.q: Why prefer failing open (allowing traffic) when the limiter backend is down for a consumer API?
options: Availability is preserved; the limiter is protection, not a correctness gate
Failing open resets every client's counters, giving all clients a clean slate afterwards
HTTP requires that requests be served whenever intermediaries fail
Failing closed would corrupt the counter store permanently

questions.q: A batch client sends 10k requests at midnight and gets throttled. Which limiter change lets it proceed smoothly?
options: A fixed window aligned exactly to midnight so the burst fits inside it
A larger bucket capacity allowing bursts while keeping the average rate
A leaky bucket with a slower drain, spreading the burst across the day
Per-IP limits, since batch jobs originate from many source addresses

questions.q: Clients retry immediately on 429, amplifying load. What server guidance most directly breaks the loop?
options: Return 500 instead so clients switch over to their error path
Blackhole the client's IP for an hour after the very first 429
Serve cached stale responses to every throttled client instead
Retry-After headers plus jittered exponential backoff in client guidance

questions.q: Why add jitter to client retry backoff?
options: To desynchronize retries so they don't arrive in synchronized waves
To make legitimate retry traffic harder for attackers to fingerprint and imitate
To ensure each client's total wait time works out exactly equal
To satisfy TCP congestion control requirements on retransmission

questions.q: Tiered limits (free vs paid). Where does the tier lookup belong?
options: In the client, which selects its own tier via a request header
In the database layer, throttling queries by table ownership
In the gateway's auth step, attaching quota attributes to the verified identity
In DNS, by resolving paying customers to a separate pool of faster endpoints

questions.q: 1M active clients with a 10 req/s limit each, sliding window log in Redis. Why does memory blow up?
options: Storing per-request timestamps costs memory proportional to allowed requests per window per client
Redis duplicates each key on every shard, squaring the total storage
TTL metadata dominates, costing roughly a megabyte per client key
Sorted sets must store the full request body alongside every entry

questions.q: Global limit of 1000 req/s across 10 gateway nodes: split local quotas vs a central counter?
options: Split quotas overshoot the global limit whenever traffic is skewed toward one node
Split quotas waste capacity under skewed traffic; central counters add latency and a failure point
Central counters can never be made atomic across nodes, so they systematically undercount by design
Split quotas require sticky sessions, which double memory usage on the balancer

questions.q: A downstream handles 5k req/s. Steady traffic is 4k with 3x spikes lasting 10s. Which limiter config fits best?
options: A fixed one-minute window of 300k requests aligned to the wall clock
A token bucket refilling at 12k/s with capacity one, matching the spike rate
A leaky bucket draining at 12k/s backed by an unbounded in-memory queue
A token bucket refilling near 5k/s with burst capacity sized to downstream headroom

questions.q: Thousands of users behind one corporate NAT constantly hit per-IP limits. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the global limit for everyone until the complaints stop arriving across all users
Switch to per-region limits derived from GeoIP lookups at the edge
Key limits on authenticated identity where available, falling back to IP
Exempt all known corporate IP ranges from rate limiting entirely
